source_text: Sed ab excessu revertar ad principalitatem veritatis et posteritatem mendacitatis disputandam ex illius quoque parabolae patrocinio quae bonum semen frumenti a domino seminatum in primore constituit, avenarum autem sterilis foeni adulterium ab inimico diabolo postea superducit. Proprie enim doctrinarum distinctionem figurat, quia et alibi verbum dei seminis similitudo est. Ita ex ipso ordine manifestatur id esse dominicum et verum quod sit prius traditum, id autem extraneum et falsum quod sit posterius inmissum. Ea sententia manebit adversus posteriores quasque haereses, quibus nulla constantia de conscientia competit ad defendendam sibi veritatem.
thought_title: The parable of wheat and weeds proves truth is prior, falsehood later
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that heretical teachings are later than the apostolic truth, and he now turns to the parable of the wheat and the weeds as evidence.
pass_a_gloss: But from the digression I will return to the priority of truth and the lateness of falsehood, to be argued also from the support of that parable which establishes the good seed of wheat sown by the Lord in the first place, but afterwards introduces the adulteration of wild oats of barren hay by the enemy the devil. For it properly figures the distinction of doctrines, because also elsewhere the word of God is a likeness of seed. Thus from the very order it is made manifest that that is the Lord's and true which was handed down first, but that is foreign and false which was let in later. That judgment will remain against all later heresies, to which no constancy from conscience belongs for defending the truth for themselves.

choices.why: Keeps the legal-temporal force of principalitas as 'being first in order', matching the argument that what is first is true.
Posteritas means 'being later'; rendering it as 'lateness' preserves the temporal contrast with priority.
The word means both adultery and adulteration; 'adulteration' fits the agricultural image of mixing bad seed into good.
Inmissum means 'sent in' or 'introduced'; 'let in' keeps the passive sense of something inserted from outside.
The phrase pairs constantia (steadfastness) with conscientia (conscience/knowledge); the literal rendering preserves the wordplay.

pass_b_english: But let me turn back from that digression to argue for the priority of truth and the lateness of falsehood, drawing support as well from that parable in which the good seed of wheat is sown first by the Lord, and afterwards the enemy, the devil, lets in the adulteration of barren wild oats and hay. For this properly pictures the distinction between doctrines, since elsewhere too the word of God is compared to seed (Luke 8:11). So the very order of things makes it clear that what was handed down first is the Lord's and is true, while what was let in later is foreign and false. That verdict will stand against every later heresy, none of which has any constancy from conscience to claim the truth for itself.
